title: Al-'Azim, the Magnificent
tomorrow: on the last day, what does God do with what you hid?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Halim, and a bucket of water instead of a shout. The line: forbearing. Today closes the first part of the Names with a word you can say with your whole body.

Phone held high at a concert, trying to fit the whole stage into the frame. It never fits. Some things are only the right size when you stop filming and just stand there. Now the odd detail, yesterday's question. In every unit of the prayer, Muslims bend forward into ruku', hands on knees, back level, head down. And in that low, small posture, the words they say are huge: subhana rabbiyal 'azim. Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent. Why the biggest word in the smallest pose?
screen: `THE STAGE NEVER FITS.` → `BENT LOW IN RUKU'.` → `THE BIGGEST WORD, THE SMALLEST POSE.`

segments.voice: The answer is a hadith. When a verse came down telling the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to glorify the name of his Lord, the Magnificent, the Prophet said: put it in your ruku'. So the phrase in the bow isn't a later habit. It's a verse, moved into the body. That's the detail to tell a friend tonight. And the puzzle solves itself. You don't bow to something your own size. The bow is the body saying what the words say: this is bigger than me. That's today's Name. Al-'Azim, the Magnificent, vaster than all. It closes Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, and Pickthall renders it this way: "He is the Sublime, the Tremendous." Tremendous is his word for 'azim. Nothing you could hold up a phone to. Here's what that does on an ordinary day. A fight, a grade, a group chat that went wrong: they feel enormous until you put them next to the Magnificent, and then they find their actual size. Not nothing. Just their size. And that hadith has a second half, about a different posture, saved for another day.
screen: `A VERSE: GLORIFY THY LORD.` · `PUT IT IN YOUR RUKU'.` · `THE SUBLIME, THE TREMENDOUS.` · `EVERYTHING FINDS ITS SIZE.` · then, large: `MAGNIFICENT.`

segments.voice: Step outside, or go to the nearest window, and look up. Find the farthest thing you can see: a cloud's edge, a star, the blinking light of a plane. Stay with it through the sit, phone down, and let whatever's been looming find its actual size.
screen: `LOOK UP.` · `THE FARTHEST THING YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Al-'Azim. The Magnificent, vaster than all, the Name said bent low in every ruku'.
Keep this: magnificent, too big for any frame, and everything else back to its real size. That's part one of the Names, complete.

howItsDone: Muslims say subhana rabbiyal 'azim, glory to my Lord the Magnificent, in the ruku' of the prayer, repeating it; the Throne Verse (2:255), which ends with al-'Azim, is recited by some after prayers and before sleep.
